hints: Think about three different ideas here, reactivity and extraction, thermal decomposition, and reaction with water.
Remember calcium is more reactive than magnesium, so ask yourself if magnesium could ever steal oxygen from calcium oxide.
Recall what happens when a Group 2 nitrate is heated and when a basic oxide like CaO meets water, then count which statements hold.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 - reduction by magnesium**

Think about who is more reactive. Calcium is above magnesium in the reactivity series, so calcium holds onto oxygen more strongly.

Reaction if it happened would be:
$$\text{CaO} + \text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{Ca}$$
This does not happen because Mg is less reactive and cannot reduce $\text{CaO}$. So statement 1 is false.

**Check statement 2 - heating calcium nitrate**

Group 2 nitrates decompose on heating to give the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Calcium is no exception.

$$2\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CaO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$
So $\text{CaO}$ is definitely produced. Statement 2 is true.

**Check statement 3 - reaction with cold water**

Calcium oxide is a basic oxide and is often called quicklime. It reacts vigorously even with cold water to make slaked lime.

$$\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$$
So statement 3 is true. With 2 and 3 true and 1 false, the correct combination is 2 and 3 only.

options.A: Incorrect because it claims 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Statements 2 and 3 are correct but 1 is false since magnesium, being less reactive than calcium, cannot reduce calcium oxide.
options.B: Incorrect because it claims 1 and 2 only. While 2 is correct, 1 is false for reactivity reasons, and it wrongly leaves out 3 which is true as CaO reacts with cold water to form Ca(OH)2.
options.C: Correct because only 2 and 3 are true. Calcium nitrate decomposes on heating to CaO, NO2 and O2, and CaO reacts with cold water to give calcium hydroxide. Statement 1 is false.
options.D: Incorrect because it claims only 1 is correct. Statement 1 is actually the false one, as a less reactive metal (Mg) cannot extract a more reactive metal (Ca) from its oxide.
